screens.title: Smart Contract Security Audits & Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Security for smart contracts is a process, not a single step. In practice you combine strong development practices, automated analysis, and independent expert reviews to manage risk. This lesson shows you what professional audits do, how tools like Slither, MythX, and Solhint fit into your workflow, when formal verification is appropriate, and the key trade-offs for upgradeable contracts. You will learn concrete examples: running Solhint on a sample contract, interpreting common warnings, and understanding proxy risks like storage collisions and unauthorized upgrades. A focused audit can find design-level logic errors that tools miss, while automated tools are fast and integrate into CI to catch common problems early. Throughout, I’ll emphasize practical decisions: when to invest in a manual audit versus relying on tooling, how to keep contracts simple and well-documented, and how to design upgradeability safely. By the end you’ll be able to plan a security lifecycle for a real contract and ask the right questions when engaging auditors.

screens.title: Professional Security Audits — What an Audit Does
screens.narratorSegment: A professional security audit is a structured, expert review of your smart contract code and design. It starts with manual code review: experienced auditors read and reason about every function, looking for logical flaws, access control gaps, and attack patterns that automated tools may miss. Auditors run automated tools as part of the process to surface common issues quickly, and then they perform threat modeling to imagine likely attack vectors and adversarial inputs. They also review documentation to ensure the code implements the intended specification and call out ambiguous behavior. The final output is a prioritized report that categorizes findings by severity, explains root causes, and provides remediation suggestions. For high-value contracts this human-led analysis is indispensable because it finds design-level errors that tooling cannot. A common misconception is that an audit guarantees safety; instead, an audit reduces risk by surfacing issues and recommending fixes, but security remains a responsibility across development, testing, and operations. Example: for a contract handling large funds, an audit will explicitly test access control on ownership and upgrade paths and will flag functions that lack require checks. The takeaway: plan audits early, provide clear docs, and treat the audit as a collaborative improvement process rather than a final stamp of approval.

keyIdea.title: Audit Purpose
keyIdea.text: A professional audit combines human insight with tooling to find complex logical and design flaws; it produces prioritized findings and remediation guidance.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Professional Audit Process
Audit Steps
A reliable audit follows repeatable stages and clear deliverables.
1. Manual Code Review
Line-by-line analysis to find logic errors, access-control gaps, and subtle vulnerabilities.
2. Automated Tooling
Run Slither, MythX, and linters to collect reproducible findings.
3. Threat Modeling
Identify likely attacker goals and design tests for those scenarios.
4. Documentation Review
Ensure code matches specification and assumptions are explicit.
Deliverables & Example
Audits produce prioritized reports and remediation steps.
Report Sections
  • Executive summary and severity breakdown
  • Detailed issue descriptions with code references
  • Recommended fixes and verification steps
Common Mistake
Treating an audit as a one-time checkbox instead of an ongoing process tied to tests and monitoring.
Key Takeaway
Use audits for high-risk contracts and provide clear documentation to maximize value from reviewers.

screens.title: Automated Security Analysis Tools
screens.narratorSegment: Automated analysis tools inspect code without executing it or they augment execution with symbolic and dynamic techniques. Slither is a static analysis framework for Solidity that flags patterns like reentrancy, integer errors, and access control issues, and it also produces control-flow hints that help an auditor reason about data paths. MythX combines static, dynamic, and symbolic analysis to broaden coverage, using fuzzing and symbolic execution to explore unusual inputs. Solhint is a linter focused on style and common best practices; while it’s not a security oracle, it flags patterns that correlate with bugs. These tools speed discovery, integrate into CI, and help maintain code quality as teams change code. But they have limits: they often miss complex business-logic flaws and can produce false positives. A common misconception is relying solely on automated outputs as proof of security; instead, treat these tools as evidence collectors that prioritize what humans should inspect next. For example, Slither might flag a function for potential reentrancy, giving you a starting point to audit the function’s effects and external calls. The right workflow combines linters in pre-commit, analyzers in CI, and manual review for the most critical findings.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Automated Tools
Tool Comparison
Slither (Static)
Detects reentrancy, improper access checks, and common Solidity pitfalls; produces control and data-flow insights.
MythX (Hybrid)
Combines static, dynamic, and symbolic execution for broader coverage, useful for CI and deeper analysis.
Solhint (Linter)
Enforces style and best practices, catches patterns that often precede vulnerabilities.
Practical Integration
How to get useful value from tools without over-relying on them.
CI Integration
Run Slither/MythX in CI to fail builds on high-severity warnings and track regressions.
Misconception
Tools find many issues but can miss business-logic and produce false positives. Use them to guide, not certify.
Example
Slither flags potential reentrancy in a withdraw function. Use that finding to manually check state updates and CEI ordering.

screens.title: Running Slither & Slither Output
screens.narratorSegment: Running Slither is a simple step that gives you a quick inventory of suspicious constructs. Install Slither with Python tooling, then invoke it on your contracts to produce a list of findings and control-flow context. For example, running Slither on a contract will return issues categorized by severity and a brief explanation for each. This output is valuable as an input to manual review — it points auditors to functions and paths that need closer inspection. A common misconception is treating every Slither finding as a confirmed vulnerability; instead, you should triage each finding by reading the reason, looking at the reported code lines, and reasoning whether the pattern is exploitable in your specific design. Concrete example: running Slither might report a suspected reentrancy issue on a withdraw function. You would then check whether the contract follows Checks-Effects-Interactions, whether it uses reentrancy guards, and whether external calls are necessary. After triage, some findings become actionable fixes and others become documented false positives. The practical discipline is to integrate Slither into CI, review new findings on pull requests, and track high-severity items in your issue tracker.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Slither Walkthrough
Install & Run
Example commands and typical output summary.
# Install Slither (requires Python)
pip install slither-analyzer

# Run Slither on a contract file
slither contracts/VulnerableEtherStore.sol

# Typical output:
# : - High - Reentrancy vulnerability - explanation...
Key Tip
Use Slither output as a prioritization map for manual review; note the file and line references it prints.
Triage Pattern
How to evaluate a finding from Slither.
1. Read the Finding
Understand the condition Slither identifies and where it occurs.
2. Reproduce in Context
Check the function’s full code path and external calls for exploitability.
3. Classify
Decide if it’s high-severity, a false positive, or informational, and document that decision.
4. Remediate & Test
Apply fixes, add unit tests, and rerun tools to verify resolution.

screens.title: Run Solhint on a Sample Contract
screens.narratorSegment: Solhint is a linter that helps enforce style and common safety patterns. In the lab you will install Solhint and run it on a provided sample contract. The linter will report warnings like missing access control on a function or uninitialized local variables. For example, Solhint might warn that transferOwnership lacks an onlyOwner modifier, indicating anyone can change the owner — a critical access-control bug. Another warning could flag an uninitialized local variable, which can lead to unexpected zero values or logic errors. The practical exercise is to run Solhint, read each reported rule, and map it to a security implication: missing access control becomes an urgent fix, while style issues might be lower priority. When you interpret output, include file and line references, then fix the contract and rerun the linter. This loop—lint, fix, test—reduces simple mistakes before they reach an auditor. A misconception to avoid is assuming linters find runtime vulnerabilities; they identify risky patterns and enforce consistency. The goal is faster feedback during development and cleaner code for auditors to review. Run Solhint on a Sample Contract means linters improve code quality and flag patterns that map to security risks, but they require developer triage and fixes.. In practical terms, install solhint and interpret typical warnings in the sample output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Solhint Lab
Install & Run
# Install Solhint
npm install -g solhint

# Run Solhint on a file
solhint contracts/SampleContract.sol

# Example warnings may include:
# 17:9  warning  Expected 'onlyOwner' modifier.  (security/no-missing-require)
# 22:12 warning  Local variable 'x' is not initialized.  (compiler-warnings/uninitialized-variables)
Practice
Run Solhint, collect warnings, and write a short remediation plan for each high-severity item.
Interpretation & Example
What the sample warnings mean and how to fix them.
Missing Access Control
If transferOwnership is public without onlyOwner, anyone can steal control. Fix by adding a proper access modifier.
Uninitialized Variable
Local variables should be explicitly initialized to avoid logic errors; set a default before returning or using the value.
Key Takeaway
Treat linter warnings as actionable prompts: fix, test, and re-run before requesting an audit.

screens.title: Formal Verification
screens.narratorSegment: Formal verification uses mathematical proofs to show that code adheres to a precise specification for all possible inputs. Unlike tests, which can only show the presence of bugs for specific cases, formal methods aim to prove the absence of certain classes of bugs under all execution paths. Tools exist to support this approach, but formal verification is resource-intensive and requires precise specifications and expertise. Use cases typically include the most critical, high-value modules such as core protocol accounting, bridges, or multi-signature vaults where the cost of error is extreme. A concrete example is proving that a token transfer function never allows unauthorized balance changes under the specified invariants. A common misconception is that formal verification makes a contract perfectly safe; rather, it guarantees correctness relative to the written specification. If the specification omits an assumption or models a behavior incorrectly, the proof does not protect against that mismatch. The practical approach is to reserve formal verification for small, critical modules, keep verified components minimal and well-specified, and combine proofs with audits and testing for the full system. The takeaway: formal verification raises assurance significantly but requires trade-offs in scope and cost.

keyIdea.title: Formal Verification Role
keyIdea.text: Formal proofs provide the highest assurance for specified properties but are costly and practical for only the most critical contract components.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Formal Verification
Formal Verification Explained
Mathematical proofs showing code matches a specification across all inputs.
What It Guarantees
Proof of correctness relative to a precise specification; eliminates classes of runtime errors covered by the spec.
When to Use
Critical, high-value modules where absolute assurance is needed and scope can be minimized.
Misconception
A verified contract is only as correct as its specification; missing assumptions will invalidate practical safety.
Example
Prove an accounting invariant: total supply equals sum of balances after every operation. This reduces many classes of bugs related to token accounting.
Key Takeaway
Use formal methods sparingly for small, critical components and combine them with audits and testing for system-level safety.

screens.title: Secure Development Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Secure smart contract development follows consistent, pragmatic principles. Keep contracts simple: smaller contracts are easier to audit and reason about. Prefer established libraries such as OpenZeppelin for common patterns like ERC20, Ownable, and ReentrancyGuard — these are battle tested and reduce reinventing safety-critical code. Follow the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern: perform checks, update state, and then interact with external contracts to avoid reentrancy. Handle external calls carefully—assume they can fail, and prefer pull-based payment designs where users withdraw funds rather than the contract pushing payments. Use Solidity 0.8.0+ to benefit from built-in overflow checks or SafeMath for older versions. Secure access control using msg. sender and role-based controls when needed; never rely on tx. origin. Test thoroughly: unit, integration, and property-based tests with high coverage. Document critical assumptions, invariants, and upgrade mechanics clearly for auditors. A common misconception is that adding more code for safety always helps; often extra complexity introduces new attack surfaces. The practical guidance is to prioritize small, well-documented modules, rely on audited libraries, and maintain a test suite that mirrors auditor checks. The core takeaway: design for auditability and replace complexity with explicit, tested components.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Best Practices
Secure Development Principles
A hierarchy of practices that reduce risk and improve auditability.
Keep Contracts Simple
Break functionality into small modules to ease reasoning and auditing.
Use Established Libraries
Leverage audited contracts for common patterns instead of custom implementations.
Checks → Effects → Interactions
Validate inputs, update state, then call external contracts to prevent reentrancy.
Handle External Calls Carefully
Assume calls can fail and prefer pull patterns for payments.
Prevent Overflows
Use Solidity 0.8.0+ or SafeMath for older compilers.
Secure Access Control
Use msg.sender based checks and role-based controls. Never rely on tx.origin.
Testing & Documentation
Write unit, integration, and property tests; document invariants and design decisions for auditors.

screens.title: Checks-Effects-Interactions & Payment Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: The Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern is a simple and powerful ordering rule: validate inputs and permissions first, then update internal state, and finally interact with external contracts. This ordering prevents many reentrancy attacks because the contract’s state has already been updated before any external call. For example, a withdraw function that reduces the user’s balance before calling an external transfer follows CEI and avoids classic reentrancy exploits. Similarly, prefer pull-over-push: rather than sending funds automatically to users, record withdrawable balances and let users withdraw them. This reduces DoS risks where an external receiver could revert or deliberately consume gas to block payments. A common misconception is that reentrancy guards alone are sufficient; while reentrancy guards help, CEI plus careful external-call handling provides clearer, auditable safety. Concrete example: if a contract uses call() to forward funds, always check the return value and avoid assuming success. Test the withdraw paths thoroughly, simulate failed external calls, and include unit tests that assert balances remain consistent. The core takeaway: ordering and payment patterns are low-cost, high-impact defenses that should be applied consistently across contract code. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Checks → Effects → Interactions
Order operations to reduce reentrancy risk.
Pattern
Checks: validate inputs and permissions. Effects: update state. Interactions: perform external calls last.
Example
Withdraw function reduces balance before transferring funds to the user, preventing reentry into the unchanged state.
Misconception
Reentrancy guards help but should not replace correct ordering and cautious external-call handling.
Pull over Push
Prefer user-initiated withdrawals to forced transfers.
Why Pull?
Pull reduces the impact of failed or malicious external receivers and isolates payment logic from state updates.
Testing
Write tests that simulate failed external calls and assert that internal invariants hold and funds remain withdrawable.
Key Takeaway
Ordering and pull payments are practical defenses with low overhead and high audit value.

screens.title: Upgradeability Patterns & Risks
screens.narratorSegment: Upgradeability allows contracts to evolve after deployment, but it introduces significant risks. The common approach uses a proxy that delegates calls to a logic (implementation) contract. Users interact with the proxy, which forwards calls to whatever logic address it points to. Transparent proxies separate admin calls from regular calls so upgrade operations are restricted, while UUPS moves upgrade logic into the implementation for gas efficiency. The primary risks include vulnerabilities in the upgrade mechanism itself, unauthorized upgrades, and storage collisions where the new logic’s storage layout differs and corrupts state. A concrete example: if the original logic stores a variable in slot one and the new logic inserts a new variable before it, the mapped storage can shift and lead to wrong balances or ownership. To mitigate these risks, use audited proxy libraries, enforce strict access control on upgrade functions, and write upgrade tests that confirm storage layout compatibility across versions. A misconception is that proxies automatically protect you; they only enable upgrades — the upgrade mechanism must itself be secure and audited. The practical guidance is to minimize mutable parts, lock down upgrade access, and test upgrade paths in staging before production.

screens.title: Security Lifecycle: From Dev to Monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: Security is a continuous lifecycle: design, code, analyze, audit, deploy, and monitor. Start by designing small modules and documenting assumptions. During development, run linters and static analyzers locally and in CI to catch issues early. Before production, schedule a professional audit for high-risk contracts; provide clear documentation and test artifacts to the auditors. After remediation and verification, deploy to testnets, run upgrade simulations if applicable, and stage the contract for production. Post-deploy, maintain monitoring, offer bug bounty programs, and periodically re-run static analysis as dependencies and compilers evolve. A concrete timeline: pre-commit linters during development, CI analyzers on PRs, a manual audit prior to mainnet deployment, and automated scheduled scans after deployment. A misconception is treating auditing as the end of security; in reality, code changes, new threats, and third-party updates require ongoing vigilance. The practical action is to embed security gates in your pipeline, document all fixes, and plan for regular re-evaluation of upgrade components and critical invariants. This lifecycle reduces surprise and keeps responsibility shared across development and operations. screens.title: Common Mistakes & How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Many security incidents arise from avoidable mistakes. A frequent error is relying solely on automated tools; they are powerful but miss complex logic flaws. Pair tools with manual review and clear documentation. Another critical mistake is missing access control, for example a transferOwnership function without an owner-only check — this enables immediate takeover. Uninitialized local variables can produce unexpected zeros or logic paths and should be initialized explicitly. Custom, unaudited upgradeability solutions are particularly dangerous; they can introduce buggy upgrade logic or storage layout issues that corrupt state. To avoid these mistakes, adopt a checklist: use linters early, triage tool findings, enforce access control on administrative functions, initialize variables, prefer audited proxy libraries, and test upgrade paths. Example: in the sample contract, add an onlyOwner modifier to transferOwnership, initialize local variables, and add unit tests that simulate unauthorized calls. A misconception to correct is thinking that adding more defensive code always helps; often simpler, well-documented designs and use of audited libraries reduce attack surface better than custom complexity. The final question to consider: what single change would most reduce risk in your current contract?

fullNarratorScript:
Security for smart contracts is a process, not a single step. In practice you combine strong development practices, automated analysis, and independent expert reviews to manage risk. This lesson shows you what professional audits do, how tools like Slither, MythX, and Solhint fit into your workflow, when formal verification is appropriate, and the key trade-offs for upgradeable contracts. You will learn concrete examples: running Solhint on a sample contract, interpreting common warnings, and understanding proxy risks like storage collisions and unauthorized upgrades. A focused audit can find design-level logic errors that tools miss, while automated tools are fast and integrate into CI to catch common problems early. Throughout, I’ll emphasize practical decisions: when to invest in a manual audit versus relying on tooling, how to keep contracts simple and well-documented, and how to design upgradeability safely. By the end you’ll be able to plan a security lifecycle for a real contract and ask the right questions when engaging auditors.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to plan and evaluate a security strategy for smart contracts. First, you will recognize when a professional audit is required and what it delivers: manual code review, threat modeling, and remediation reports. Second, you will use and interpret automated tools such as Slither, MythX, and Solhint in a CI pipeline to catch common vulnerabilities early. Third, you will explain what formal verification does, when it’s worth the cost, and which contract components benefit most from mathematical proofs. Finally, you will summarize secure development best practices, including the CEI pattern, using audited libraries, and safe upgradeability choices. Each objective is practical: you’ll run Solhint on a sample contract, read real warnings, and critique upgrade patterns for storage safety. These skills will help you allocate limited security budget to the highest-impact areas and avoid common pitfalls that lead to loss of funds.

This lab-focused objective slide explains the concrete actions you will take. You will install and run Solhint on a sample contract, read warnings, and map each warning to its security implication. You will run Slither to gather static findings and control/data-flow hints, and you will see how MythX augments analysis with fuzzing and symbolic checks. You will also create an audit checklist, identify which functions need access control, and practice documenting assumptions that auditors will check. Finally, you will reason about upgradeability: design a simple proxy pattern, test a mock upgrade, and list the tests needed to verify storage layout safety. These exercises emphasize tools + human review: automated tools speed discovery, but manual inspection and clear documentation drive correct remediation. You’ll leave with concrete artifacts: Solhint output interpretation, a checklist for audits, and a short upgradeability test plan.

A professional security audit is a structured, expert review of your smart contract code and design. It starts with manual code review: experienced auditors read and reason about every function, looking for logical flaws, access control gaps, and attack patterns that automated tools may miss. Auditors run automated tools as part of the process to surface common issues quickly, and then they perform threat modeling to imagine likely attack vectors and adversarial inputs. They also review documentation to ensure the code implements the intended specification and call out ambiguous behavior. The final output is a prioritized report that categorizes findings by severity, explains root causes, and provides remediation suggestions. For high-value contracts this human-led analysis is indispensable because it finds design-level errors that tooling cannot. A common misconception is that an audit guarantees safety; instead, an audit reduces risk by surfacing issues and recommending fixes, but security remains a responsibility across development, testing, and operations. Example: for a contract handling large funds, an audit will explicitly test access control on ownership and upgrade paths and will flag functions that lack require checks. The takeaway: plan audits early, provide clear docs, and treat the audit as a collaborative improvement process rather than a final stamp of approval.

Automated analysis tools inspect code without executing it or they augment execution with symbolic and dynamic techniques. Slither is a static analysis framework for Solidity that flags patterns like reentrancy, integer errors, and access control issues, and it also produces control-flow hints that help an auditor reason about data paths. MythX combines static, dynamic, and symbolic analysis to broaden coverage, using fuzzing and symbolic execution to explore unusual inputs. Solhint is a linter focused on style and common best practices; while it’s not a security oracle, it flags patterns that correlate with bugs. These tools speed discovery, integrate into CI, and help maintain code quality as teams change code. But they have limits: they often miss complex business-logic flaws and can produce false positives. A common misconception is relying solely on automated outputs as proof of security; instead, treat these tools as evidence collectors that prioritize what humans should inspect next. For example, Slither might flag a function for potential reentrancy, giving you a starting point to audit the function’s effects and external calls. The right workflow combines linters in pre-commit, analyzers in CI, and manual review for the most critical findings.

Running Slither is a simple step that gives you a quick inventory of suspicious constructs. Install Slither with Python tooling, then invoke it on your contracts to produce a list of findings and control-flow context. For example, running Slither on a contract will return issues categorized by severity and a brief explanation for each. This output is valuable as an input to manual review — it points auditors to functions and paths that need closer inspection. A common misconception is treating every Slither finding as a confirmed vulnerability; instead, you should triage each finding by reading the reason, looking at the reported code lines, and reasoning whether the pattern is exploitable in your specific design. Concrete example: running Slither might report a suspected reentrancy issue on a withdraw function. You would then check whether the contract follows Checks-Effects-Interactions, whether it uses reentrancy guards, and whether external calls are necessary. After triage, some findings become actionable fixes and others become documented false positives. The practical discipline is to integrate Slither into CI, review new findings on pull requests, and track high-severity items in your issue tracker.

Solhint is a linter that helps enforce style and common safety patterns. In the lab you will install Solhint and run it on a provided sample contract. The linter will report warnings like missing access control on a function or uninitialized local variables. For example, Solhint might warn that transferOwnership lacks an onlyOwner modifier, indicating anyone can change the owner — a critical access-control bug. Another warning could flag an uninitialized local variable, which can lead to unexpected zero values or logic errors. The practical exercise is to run Solhint, read each reported rule, and map it to a security implication: missing access control becomes an urgent fix, while style issues might be lower priority. When you interpret output, include file and line references, then fix the contract and rerun the linter. This loop—lint, fix, test—reduces simple mistakes before they reach an auditor. A misconception to avoid is assuming linters find runtime vulnerabilities; they identify risky patterns and enforce consistency. The goal is faster feedback during development and cleaner code for auditors to review. In practical terms, install solhint and interpret typical warnings in the sample output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Formal verification uses mathematical proofs to show that code adheres to a precise specification for all possible inputs. Unlike tests, which can only show the presence of bugs for specific cases, formal methods aim to prove the absence of certain classes of bugs under all execution paths. Tools exist to support this approach, but formal verification is resource-intensive and requires precise specifications and expertise. Use cases typically include the most critical, high-value modules such as core protocol accounting, bridges, or multi-signature vaults where the cost of error is extreme. A concrete example is proving that a token transfer function never allows unauthorized balance changes under the specified invariants. A common misconception is that formal verification makes a contract perfectly safe; rather, it guarantees correctness relative to the written specification. If the specification omits an assumption or models a behavior incorrectly, the proof does not protect against that mismatch. The practical approach is to reserve formal verification for small, critical modules, keep verified components minimal and well-specified, and combine proofs with audits and testing for the full system. The takeaway: formal verification raises assurance significantly but requires trade-offs in scope and cost.

Secure smart contract development follows consistent, pragmatic principles. Keep contracts simple: smaller contracts are easier to audit and reason about. Prefer established libraries such as OpenZeppelin for common patterns like ERC20, Ownable, and ReentrancyGuard — these are battle tested and reduce reinventing safety-critical code. Follow the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern: perform checks, update state, and then interact with external contracts to avoid reentrancy. Handle external calls carefully—assume they can fail, and prefer pull-based payment designs where users withdraw funds rather than the contract pushing payments. Use Solidity 0.8.0+ to benefit from built-in overflow checks or SafeMath for older versions. Secure access control using msg. sender and role-based controls when needed; never rely on tx. origin. Test thoroughly: unit, integration, and property-based tests with high coverage. Document critical assumptions, invariants, and upgrade mechanics clearly for auditors. A common misconception is that adding more code for safety always helps; often extra complexity introduces new attack surfaces. The practical guidance is to prioritize small, well-documented modules, rely on audited libraries, and maintain a test suite that mirrors auditor checks. The core takeaway: design for auditability and replace complexity with explicit, tested components.

The Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern is a simple and powerful ordering rule: validate inputs and permissions first, then update internal state, and finally interact with external contracts. This ordering prevents many reentrancy attacks because the contract’s state has already been updated before any external call. For example, a withdraw function that reduces the user’s balance before calling an external transfer follows CEI and avoids classic reentrancy exploits. Similarly, prefer pull-over-push: rather than sending funds automatically to users, record withdrawable balances and let users withdraw them. This reduces DoS risks where an external receiver could revert or deliberately consume gas to block payments. Concrete example: if a contract uses call() to forward funds, always check the return value and avoid assuming success.
